1:
The first verse is read as praise by some, as rebuke by others. John Wesley takes it wholly well: a man who through desire of wisdom has withdrawn from the noise and business of the world seeks and intermeddles with all wisdom. Charles Ellicott takes it wholly ill, rendering it that the separatist seeks his own desire and shows his teeth against all improvement: a man of small mind who follows his own narrow aims, holds aloof from men of wider views, and opposes their plans, seeing nothing in them but mischief. Keil and Delitzsch agree, rejecting an emendation that would make him one pushed aside seeking a pretext for revenge; the word denotes a man who withdraws willingly and obstinately. John Gill and Matthew Henry report both readings without choosing. Henry states the rebuke first, that men who take pride in separating from the sentiments of others and advancing notions of their own do it to gratify a lust of vain-glory; then the praise, that we must retire from the noise of the world and take pains to improve ourselves.

Adam Clarke refuses to settle it: the old versions blame the man who seeks pretences to break with his friend, and an older English Bible has whoever takes pleasure in sowing discord picking a quarrel in everything. His own nearest rendering is that he who is separated shall seek the object of his desire and mingle himself with all essential knowledge, which he says appears the best meaning.

The second verse carries it forward. Henry allows that a fool may pretend to understanding but has no true delight in it, since no progress is made in learning or religion when they are a drudgery; his only design is something to make a show with. Clarke proposes another construction, that a fool does not delight in understanding though it should manifest itself: the separated man seeks it in every hidden thing and feels his toil repaid, while the other disregards it though its springs be laid open. Ellicott puts it briefly: he does not prize understanding for itself.

At the third verse Keil and Delitzsch report a textual dispute. Most modern critics repoint the opening word so that contempt becomes a consequence of godlessness, but the received text and all the old translators make it a person coming, and they adhere to that, the noun naming not the first thing godlessness effects but the first that proceeds from it. Henry finds a double sense: the wicked are scornful and put contempt on others, and are shameful and bring contempt on themselves, so that whoever would secure his honour must retain his virtue. Clarke would rather read that when the wicked comes contempt comes, and with ignominy reproach, adding that a wicked man is despised even by the wicked.

The fourth verse turns on whether a word must be supplied. Gill, Wesley and Ellicott take the man for a wise man, and Clarke says his sayings are like deep waters, which however much you draw off do not seem to be lessened. Keil and Delitzsch object that supplying it adds what is unnecessary and omits what is needed, the noun denoting a valiant man rather than a man as he ought to be; they dismiss another scholar’s heart-words of many as unbiblical, and note that the Greek read a different text. Henry reverses the images, taking the similitudes to be elegantly transposed: the wellspring of wisdom is the deep water, which makes no noise but never runs dry, while the words are the flowing brook, watering those about him as brooks do the low grounds. Clarke ends on a variant, that eight collated manuscripts read a vein of lives for a vein of wisdom, which the Greek and Arabic support, the figure of the heart driving blood through the great artery being a favourite with this writer and his father.
5:
Matthew Henry finds two ways of perverting judgment in the fifth verse: conniving at a man’s crimes because of his dignity or wealth, and giving a cause against equity because the party is poor or a stranger. Whatever excuses men make, he says, it is an offence to God: the merits of a cause must be regarded, not the person. Adam Clarke says the same in a line: riches, influence and office count for nothing in a judicial case. Keil and Delitzsch work on the two verbs. To accept a face is in itself no wrong, meaning only to find a person agreeable; but in a judge it becomes sinful partiality. The second verb they take two ways, as a turning aside so that the righteous does not attain his right, or as an oppression, the phrase for perverting justice being transferred to the person who suffers it.

At the sixth verse Henry counts three mischiefs a fool does himself. He embroils himself in quarrels, advancing notions that others feel bound to oppose, or using provoking language; a wise man may be drawn into a quarrel against his will, but only a fool enters one by choice, and repents it too late. He exposes himself to correction, having said what deserves strokes and still saying what needs restraining. And he involves himself in ruin, his mouth proving at length his own destruction, so that his defence becomes his offence. Keil and Delitzsch render the first clause that the lips of the fool engage in strife, and observe that the stripes he calls for are those he carries off himself, since the thing goes from words to blows; the Greek, they note, read a bolder text, that his mouth calls for death. John Gill reports the Greek differently, that the lips of a fool lead him to evils; Charles Ellicott says the strokes are provoked by his insolence.

The eighth verse divides them sharply. Gill lists the possibilities and settles on the last: the words are wounds; or as the words of men who are wounded, since the talebearer pretends to be pained by what he reports; or secret, wounding behind the back; or smooth and flattering; or, as the Arabic signifies and one scholar has shown, greedily swallowed down, which is how Gill renders it. Henry keeps both text and margin. The talebearers look as if wounded by what they tell, whereas really they rejoice in the iniquity and tell it with pride; the pill being gilded, the words go down as poison. Yet taken as wounds they are deep and deadly, wounding the man of whom they are spoken in his credit and the man to whom they are spoken in his charity. Ellicott prefers the dainty morsels, eagerly swallowed and treasured in the deepest recesses of the heart to be brought out when occasion serves; John Wesley keeps the other side in three words, that they wound mortally.

Keil and Delitzsch take the disputed participle at length. Four scholars, they say, are constrained to read the second clause as a contrast and so give the word unwarranted meanings, rendering it a burning, or as whispering, or as sporting, or like soft airs; all are without support, since the word means, as the Arabic warrants, to swallow down. A fifth, that they are swallowed because spoken with reserve, they reject on the same ground. Clarke agrees on the swallowing and illustrates it most vividly. He gives the older English renderings, the words of the double-tongued and of a slanderer, then adopts the Arabic sense and compares such words to dainties eagerly swallowed because inviting to the taste: gingerbread gilded with a leaf that is a preparation of copper, or sweetmeats powdered with seeds coloured by red lead, both ruinous to the tender bowels of the poor little innocents, and both greedily swallowed for their sweetness and inviting colour.
9:
Matthew Henry pairs the figures of the ninth verse. Prodigality is bad husbandry, and those who spend more than they can afford must account for the talents entrusted to them; but idleness is no better, for the man whose hands hang down is own brother to the waster, one scattering what he has and the other letting it run through his fingers. He carries it into religion: a man careless in praying and hearing is brother to the man who does not pray or hear at all, since omissions of duty are as fatal to the soul as commissions of sin. Charles Ellicott puts it briefly, that neglect of duty causes almost as much mischief as active wickedness, and Adam Clarke makes both men destroyers. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the words: the noun means properly a commission given by another, as a king sends a messenger, and so any business a man takes in hand; the slack man produces destruction by his negligence as truly as the other does directly.

On the strong tower the voices converge but define the name variously. John Gill offers two senses, the attributes by which God is known, or else God himself, and applies the phrase to the Messiah, as an older Jewish authority does. Ellicott takes it for the titles by which God has made himself known, in which the righteous takes refuge and is lifted above the trouble that seemed ready to overwhelm him. Keil and Delitzsch go furthest: the name is the Revelation of God and the God of Revelation himself, his nature representing itself and so capable of being named, a high tower that bids defiance to every assault. Henry works the figure on both sides: there is rest in the tower for the weary and sanctuary for the pursued, while the righteous by faith and prayer run into it as their city of refuge, going out of themselves and dwelling in God and God in them. Clarke compares what a fortress is to the besieged, and John Wesley defines the name as the Lord revealed in his works and promises.

The eleventh verse turns the figure against the rich man, and here Keil and Delitzsch are severe on the versions. The word for conceit comes, they say, from a root meaning to pierce or fix, so that it means an image as a medal and then the image formed in the heart; the translators from the Greek down to the later versions wrongly thought of a different root meaning to entertain, and only one late version renders it rightly as in his fancy. Henry sets the two verses side by side: having described the firm defence of the righteous, the writer shows the false one, the rich man’s wealth being as much his confidence, and expected to do as much for him, as a godly man expects from God. He makes his wealth a city where he dwells and rules with self-complacency, entrenches himself in it and sets danger at defiance, his wealth being his wall; but it is high only in his own conceit, like a house built on sand that fails the builder when he most needs it.

Keil and Delitzsch tie the twelfth verse to the eleventh, its halves varying two earlier proverbs. Henry states both halves as forerunners: pride is the presage of ruin and ruin the punishment of pride, for before destruction men are commonly so infatuated by the just judgment of God that they grow more haughty than ever, so that their ruin may be the sorer; and humility is the presage of honour, honour being at length its reward. That, he adds, has need to be often said which men are so loth to believe. Gill applies it to the rich, who are apt to be highminded, and observes that the word rendered destruction signifies a breach that is near.
13:
Matthew Henry traces the fault of the thirteenth verse to pride. Some think it their honour to take up a cause suddenly and, having heard one side, reckon the matter too plain to need the other; but a ready wit does not do the business that solid judgment does. It is folly to pass sentence on a matter one has not the patience to enquire into, and being folly it is and will be shame. Adam Clarke makes it a matter of manners: before a man can tell out his story another begins his, and before he has answered the other confutes him piecemeal; such men, he says, are ill-bred. John Gill divides the fault in two, impatience that cannot wait for the speaker to finish and rashness that answers without weighing.

The fourteenth verse produces a real disagreement about the wounded spirit. Henry takes it of the deepest griefs: outward troubles in body, name and estate are tolerable while the mind is at ease, but the grievances of the spirit make sore the very shoulders that should carry the rest, Wounded spirits cannot help themselves, nor do others know how to help them, so it is wisdom to keep conscience void of offence. Clarke agrees, asking what can sustain a man when slow-consuming care has shot the dagger into the soul, and answering that nothing can but the unseen God. Charles Ellicott expressly excludes that case: the wounded spirit is not one crushed with the sense of sin, for God will lift that one up, but one that retires into itself and nurses its griefs. John Wesley is with Henry and Clarke, glossing it as dejected with the sense of its own guilt. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar, observing that the word for spirit takes two genders and the change here is in the highest degree characteristic, the courageous spirit that endures sickness standing in the masculine and the broken one not. Gill describes the endurance, a man bearing up under bodily infirmity, loss of substance and persecution with an undaunted spirit.

At the fifteenth verse Henry observes that the prudent never think they have prudence enough, and the more prudent a man is the more inquisitive he will be; knowledge must be got not into the head only but into the heart. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point from the two organs named: a heart vigorous in embracing knowledge is above all necessary, and the wise, already possessing it, still strive to increase it, their ear asking where more is to be found.

The sixteenth verse divides them squarely. Henry reads the gift as a bribe. a present will go far towards a man’s liberty, since courtiers who use their interest even for oppressed innocence expect a gratuity, and far towards his preferment; the world is corrupt indeed when gifts gain men what they are unworthy of, and no wonder that those take bribes in office who gave bribes for it. He ends by blessing the Lord, who makes us welcome to come to his throne without money and without price. Clarke reads it the same way, calling it a base practice to bring a present to the great man whose presence one enters, without which there is no audience and no justice; he derives it from the rule that no one approaches the altar of God without an offering, potentates wishing to be counted petty gods having demanded the like. Keil and Delitzsch deny the sense of a bribe: the word is an indifferent one, and the proverb means that a man clears a path for himself by showing himself liberal rather than niggardly, as their own saying has it that with hat in hand one goes through the whole land. Ellicott agrees, calling it judicious liberality, and Gill takes it of a man enlarged out of straits or given access to a judge.
17:
The seventeenth verse repeats the caution of the thirteenth in court. Matthew Henry puts it as a maxim, that one tale is good till another is told: the first speaker tells a straight story and relates only what makes for him, so that the defendant must be heard and allowed to cross-examine. We have two ears, he says, and it is well to listen even to enemies, that we may form a better judgment of ourselves. Adam Clarke says the same: a man makes out a fair tale at first, having the choice of circumstances, but his neighbour dissects it and cross-questions every witness. Charles Ellicott reads the neighbour as the adversary in the suit, and John Gill finds the thing true in private conversation and theological controversy as well as in lawsuits. Keil and Delitzsch take it as an exhortation to caution, not to justify without more ado the man who speaks first; the clause, they note, may be construed two ways, and the accentuation rightly leaves it undecided.

On the lot Henry has the boldest suggestion here. Contentions happen chiefly among the mighty, jealous for their honour, while the poor are forced to be peaceable; but even their contentions may be ended by lot, and sometimes better so than by endless argument. Canaan was divided by lot to prevent quarrels, and if the use of lots in games had not profaned this appeal to Providence, he thinks it might decide many controversies now, done with prayer and due solemnity: if the law be a lottery, as some have called it, it were as well that a lottery were the law. Keil and Delitzsch supply the reason: the mighty are not opponents who maintain their cause with weighty arguments, but men who without the lot would make good their demands by blows, so that the lot, as the judgment of God, brings peace in place of force. Gill notes that the lot is used when a case can be settled neither privately nor in court.

The nineteenth verse turns on a disputed reading, and the sides are directly opposed. Clarke reports that almost all the versions make it a brother assisted by a brother, like a fortified city, and quotes the fable of the dying father, his sons and the bundle of faggots, concluding that unity among brethren makes them invincible. Keil and Delitzsch reject it, since the verb does not properly mean to be helped but to be saved, and praise instead a rendering they call among its author’s happiest, that a brother wounded resists more than a strong city and strife more than palace bolts. Ellicott would render the participle wronged rather than offended, the contentions of former friends being like a castle’s bars. Gill agrees that a fortified city may sooner be taken than one brother reconciled to another, since love turned to hatred is the more bitter. Henry draws the counsel: quarrels among relations are to be prevented, since between such persons things are taken most unkindly, and though wisdom would make forgiveness easy, corruption makes it hardest there; yet Esau, a brother offended, seemed harder to be won than a strong city and was won.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the twentieth verse as closing the series, reading it as the reaction of speech upon the speaker: he tastes in rich measure the consequences not of his good words only but of whatever he has spoken, an oxymoron like the saying that not what goes into the mouth but what comes out defiles a man. Henry takes the belly for the conscience and makes a man’s comfort depend on its testimony, which will be for or against him according as he has governed his tongue. John Wesley puts it in a line, that wise discourses satisfy the speaker as well as profit the hearer; Clarke, that our own words frequently shape our fortune in life.
21:
The twenty-first verse gives the tongue a power the commentators are careful to define. John Gill distributes it among witnesses, judges and teachers, who by speaking well or ill bring death or life on themselves and others. Adam Clarke applies it to public pleaders, on whose tongues life and death may hang. Matthew Henry shifts the weight to the affections behind the speech: he who loves to speak aright, of choice and with delight, finds life in it, while he who loves to speak amiss finds death. Keil and Delitzsch find the clause obscure. All refer the loving to the tongue, they say, but to love the tongue is a strange expression; one takes it of the man who loves to babble, another of the man who guards it carefully, a third combines the two. Charles Ellicott settles it briefly as loving to use it.

At the next verse the question is whether a word must be supplied. Gill takes the wife to be a good one, as the old versions supply it; Henry says a bad wife deserves no name of such honour, and Ellicott and John Wesley require one who deserves it. Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch refuse the addition. Clarke observes that none of the versions but one is pleased with the naked simplicity of the Hebrew, and that although a few copies carry the adjective, that authority is too slender to justify changing the text. The Hebrew as it stands, he says, teaches a general doctrine, marriage with all its troubles being a blessing from God. Keil and Delitzsch put the same case on literary grounds: gnomic brevity and force disdain such enervating adjectives and cautious limitations of the idea.

On the poor and the rich the voices press different sides of one contrast. Henry finds a use in poverty, which often humbles the spirit and mortifies pride, teaching men that when necessity forces them to beg they must not prescribe or demand. On the other side a prosperous condition often makes men imperious, and he calls it a foolish humour in some rich men to think their riches warrant them in giving hard words, whereas gentlemen ought to be gentle. Keil and Delitzsch note that eastern proverbial poetry delights in this contrast, and read the verse both as a consolation to the poor, to whom nothing unusual happens when a rich man insults, and as a warning to the rich not to be divested of humanity by mammon. Ellicott compresses it to a warning against the hardening of riches.

The last verse is the most disputed, and Keil and Delitzsch overturn the received sense of it. The opening word is read by some versions as there is rather than a man; they defend the other reading, noting that the Masoretic scholars listed this among the places where a reader is liable to err, and render it: a man of many friends comes off a loser, but there is a friend more faithful than a brother. Clarke reports the same disorder among the critics, calling the original obscure, and sets out four renderings, one making the man of friends ring again in boasting, another making him ready to be ruined; he adds that the two closing verses are wanting in the Greek and Arabic. On the second clause he is blunt: many apply it to God or to Christ, but the text has no such meaning. Henry applies it exactly so, and Gill goes further still, finding the Father, the Son and the Spirit all friends of the believer. On the first clause the two agree: friendship must be cultivated, Clarke saying that love begets love and a man who does not maintain a friendly carriage cannot expect to keep his friends, while Henry observes that a friend no kin to us may prove stronger in the trial than a brother.
